questions.stem: Regarding the receptors in the skin:

options.label: A
options.text: all skin receptor are encapsulated

options.label: B
options.text: the receptive fields of touch receptors are uniform in area

options.label: C
options.text: the nociceptors of the skin are bare nerve endings

options.label: D
options.text: sensory information from the skin reaches the brain via the dorsal pathway

options.label: E
options.text: sensory information from the skin is stored in the hypothalamus

questions.why: Cutaneous nociceptors usually end as unencapsulated branches of sensory axons. They respond to potentially damaging mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli and transmit signals through A-delta or C fibres.

notes.A: Some touch receptors have specialised capsules, but free nerve endings are also common in skin.
notes.B: Receptive field size varies with receptor type and location. Fingertips often have smaller fields than the trunk.
notes.D: Discriminative touch can ascend in the dorsal columns. Much pain and temperature information travels in the anterolateral system.
notes.E: Cutaneous signals are relayed through several pathways to the brain. The hypothalamus participates in autonomic regulation rather than serving as general sensory storage.

questions.stem: The large onion-shaped receptors deep in the dermis and in subcutaneous tissue, which respond to deep pressure are:

options.label: A
options.text: Merkel discs

options.label: B
options.text: Pacinian corpuscles

options.label: C
options.text: free nerve endings

options.label: D
options.text: muscle spindles

options.label: E
options.text: stretch receptors

questions.why: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric connective-tissue layers surrounding a sensory ending. They lie in deep dermis or subcutaneous tissue and respond best to rapid changes in pressure and high-frequency vibration.

notes.A: Merkel cell–neurite complexes are superficial, slowly adapting receptors for sustained indentation, edges and texture.
notes.C: Free nerve endings are unencapsulated, unlike Pacinian corpuscles. Many mediate pain, temperature or itch.
notes.D: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors within skeletal muscle, where they monitor muscle length and changes in length.
notes.E: Skin stretch is associated particularly with slowly adapting mechanoreceptors. It does not identify the large lamellated pressure and vibration receptor.

questions.stem: Which skin receptors are the most numerous?

options.label: A
options.text: pain receptors

options.label: B
options.text: heat receptors

options.label: C
options.text: cold receptors

options.label: D
options.text: proprioceptors

options.label: E
options.text: stretch receptors

questions.why: Nociceptors are widespread and numerous in skin. Their branching free endings detect potentially harmful mechanical, thermal and chemical stimuli. Receptor density and the relative numbers vary with the site and the method used to count them.

notes.B: Warmth-sensitive afferents are a specialised subset. They are less widely distributed than the broader population of cutaneous nociceptive endings.
notes.C: Cold spots can outnumber warm spots in many skin regions, but they represent one thermal modality and are not the broadest group listed.
notes.D: The principal proprioceptors are muscle spindles and tendon organs, not the dominant receptors in the skin.
notes.E: Skin stretch is sensed by a subset of cutaneous mechanoreceptors. It does not account for the many free endings that detect noxious stimulation.

questions.stem: Which two body areas were least sensitive to touch?

options.label: A
options.text: neck and shoulders

options.label: B
options.text: back of calf and back of neck

options.label: C
options.text: palm of hand and back of hand

options.label: D
options.text: lips and fingertips

options.label: E
options.text: chest and abdomen

questions.why: Areas with the largest receptive fields (and fewest touch receptors per unit area) like the back and calf are least sensitive.

notes.A: The neck is moderately sensitive.
notes.C: The palm is very sensitive.
notes.D: These are the MOST sensitive areas.
notes.E: More sensitive than the calf and the back of the neck.

questions.stem: Which of these neurotransmitters is primarily responsible for natural pain relief in the body?

options.label: A
options.text: NE

options.label: B
options.text: substance P

options.label: C
options.text: dopamine

options.label: D
options.text: serotonin

options.label: E
options.text: beta-endorphins

questions.why: Beta-endorphin is an endogenous opioid peptide that activates opioid receptors and can reduce nociceptive transmission. Natural pain modulation also involves other opioid peptides and descending noradrenergic and serotonergic pathways.

notes.A: Noradrenaline can inhibit nociceptive transmission in descending pathways, but it is not an endogenously produced opioid peptide.
notes.B: Substance P is released by some nociceptive afferents and can help transmit or amplify pain signals in the spinal cord.
notes.C: Dopamine can influence motivation, salience and pain processing. It is not the classic endogenous opioid mediator among these choices.
notes.D: Serotonergic pathways can alter spinal pain transmission, sometimes in either direction. Beta-endorphin provides the direct opioid example here.

questions.stem: Pain receptors in the gut and urinary tract may be stimulated by:

options.label: A
options.text: distention

options.label: B
options.text: inflammation of the wall

options.label: C
options.text: acid fluid

options.label: D
options.text: vigorous rhythmic contractions behind an obstruction

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Visceral afferents can respond to excessive stretch, strong contraction, inflammation and chemical irritation. An obstruction can activate several of these mechanisms by increasing wall tension and provoking contractions above the blockage.

notes.A: Excessive distension increases tension in the organ wall and can activate mechanically sensitive visceral afferents.
notes.B: Inflammation releases mediators that can excite or sensitise nociceptive afferents in the wall.
notes.C: Acid can irritate some visceral mucosa and activate chemosensitive afferents. Normal acidic fluid alone does not necessarily cause pain.
notes.D: Strong contractions against an obstruction raise wall tension and can produce intermittent, colicky pain.

questions.stem: Visceral pain:

options.label: A
options.text: is poorly localized compared with pain arising in skin

options.label: B
options.text: is often felt in the mid line

options.label: C
options.text: may cause reflex contraction of overlying skeletal muscle

options.label: D
options.text: may cause reflex vomiting

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Visceral pain is often diffuse or referred because visceral sensory input is sparse and converges with somatic input in the spinal cord. It can be felt in the midline and may be accompanied by muscle guarding or autonomic responses such as vomiting.

notes.A: Cutaneous sensory input is mapped more precisely than visceral input, so visceral pain is generally harder to localise.
notes.B: Pain from many midline viscera is first perceived near the midline, although referred and localised patterns also occur.
notes.C: Visceral afferent activity can evoke reflex contraction of nearby skeletal muscle, such as abdominal wall guarding.
notes.D: Visceral sensory signals can activate brainstem and autonomic pathways that cause nausea or vomiting.

questions.stem: Headache can be caused by:

options.label: A
options.text: dilatation of intracranial blood vessels

options.label: B
options.text: meningeal irritation

options.label: C
options.text: blood in the cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: D
options.text: loss of cerebrospinal fluid following lumbar puncture

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Headache can arise when pain-sensitive intracranial vessels or meninges are stimulated. Meningeal inflammation, subarachnoid blood, changes in vascular tone and low cerebrospinal fluid pressure can all contribute in different conditions.

notes.A: Dilatation or other vascular changes can stimulate pain-sensitive structures in some headaches. Vessel calibre is not the only mechanism.
notes.B: Meningeal irritation activates sensory afferents and can cause a severe headache.
notes.C: Blood in the subarachnoid space can irritate the meninges and cause sudden severe head pain.
notes.D: A persistent cerebrospinal fluid leak after lumbar puncture can reduce pressure and produce a positional headache.

questions.stem: Severe pain may lead to:

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in blood pressure due to a fall in vascular resistance in skeletal muscle

options.label: B
options.text: a fall in heart rate due to an increase in cardiac vagal tone

options.label: C
options.text: vomiting through a reflex centre in the brainstem

options.label: D
options.text: profuse sweating due to activation of sympathetic nerves

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Severe pain can trigger sweating and nausea through autonomic and brainstem pathways. It can also precipitate a vasovagal episode, in which withdrawal of vasoconstrictor tone and increased cardiac vagal activity can lower blood pressure and heart rate.

notes.A: A vasovagal response can decrease vascular resistance in skeletal muscle and other beds, reducing arterial pressure.
notes.B: Increased cardiac vagal drive can slow the heart during a vasovagal episode.
notes.C: Nociceptive and autonomic inputs can activate brainstem circuits that coordinate nausea and vomiting.
notes.D: Sympathetic cholinergic activity can stimulate eccrine sweat glands during severe pain.

questions.stem: Regarding the focusing of the eye:

options.label: A
options.text: hypermetropia may be corrected by diverging lens

options.label: B
options.text: the focus of the eye is controlled by parasympathetic innervation of the ciliary body

options.label: C
options.text: the lens is the chief refractive element of the eye

options.label: D
options.text: when the eye focuses on a distant object the ciliary muscle contracts

options.label: E
options.text: the focus of the eye is controlled by sympathetic innervation of the ciliary body

questions.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the oculomotor pathway stimulate the ciliary muscle for near accommodation. Its contraction reduces zonular tension and lets the lens become more convex, increasing refractive power.

notes.A: Hypermetropia is corrected with a converging lens, which moves the focal point forward onto the retina.
notes.C: The cornea accounts for most of the eye's total refractive power. The lens provides the adjustable component.
notes.D: For distant vision the ciliary muscle is relatively relaxed, allowing the zonules to flatten the lens.
notes.E: Sympathetic activity helps dilate the pupil. The principal active control of near accommodation is parasympathetic.

questions.stem: Regarding the physiology of the eye:

options.label: A
options.text: the intraocular pressure is about 1,5 mm Hg

options.label: B
options.text: when light is directed to one eye, both pupils constrict

options.label: C
options.text: the pupils dilate when the eye is focused on a near object

options.label: D
options.text: the aqueous humor is an ultrafiltrate of plasma

options.label: E
options.text: the pupils constrict when the eye is focused on a distant object

questions.why: Light in one eye normally causes both direct and consensual pupil constriction. Retinal input reaches the pretectal region, which activates parasympathetic pathways from both Edinger–Westphal nuclei to the pupillary sphincters.

notes.A: Normal intraocular pressure is usually substantially above 1.5 mm Hg and commonly lies around 10–21 mm Hg.
notes.C: Near fixation typically produces pupil constriction along with convergence and an increase in lens power.
notes.D: Aqueous humour formation involves diffusion and ultrafiltration, but secretion across the ciliary epithelium accounts for most production.
notes.E: The near response constricts the pupil. Distance fixation does not elicit this same accommodation-associated constriction.

questions.stem: Regarding vision:

options.label: A
options.text: protanopes cannot distinguish between red and green because they lack the pigment for detecting green light

options.label: B
options.text: full colour vision is possible in dim light

options.label: C
options.text: full dark adaptation takes nearly 30 min

options.label: D
options.text: in a dark-adapted eye, the visual activity is best in the centre of the visual field

options.label: E
options.text: in the retina there are more ganglion cells than photoreceptors

questions.why: Cone sensitivity improves first after entering darkness, followed by a slower increase in rod sensitivity as photopigment regenerates. Near-full dark adaptation can take about 30 minutes, depending on prior illumination.

notes.A: Protanopia results from lack of functional long-wavelength cone pigment. Loss of medium-wavelength cone function characterises deuteranopia.
notes.B: In dim light, rod signals dominate and colour discrimination is poor because rods do not distinguish wavelengths by themselves.
notes.D: The central fovea is rod-free. In very dim light, viewing a faint object slightly off-centre can make it easier to see.
notes.E: Photoreceptors are far more numerous than retinal ganglion cells. Many photoreceptors can converge onto downstream retinal pathways.

questions.stem: In the lens:

options.label: A
options.text: potassium concentration is higher than that of sodium

options.label: B
options.text: the majority of the lens proteins are water soluble

options.label: C
options.text: there is a high concentration of reduced glutathione

options.label: D
options.text: glutathione is decreased in the presence of cataract

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: The healthy lens maintains more intracellular potassium than sodium and contains abundant soluble crystallins. Reduced glutathione helps protect lens proteins from oxidation. Its depletion is associated with cataract formation.

notes.A: Lens cell transport maintains relatively high potassium and low sodium, helping preserve hydration and transparency.
notes.B: Water-soluble crystallins account for much of the normal lens protein. Cataract can increase the insoluble protein fraction.
notes.C: Reduced glutathione is an important lens antioxidant that protects protein thiol groups.
notes.D: Reduced glutathione can fall in cataract, particularly in the lens nucleus, where oxidative damage accumulates.

questions.stem: Vitamin A is a precursor for the synthesis of:

options.label: A
options.text: somatostatin

options.label: B
options.text: retinine-1

options.label: C
options.text: the pigment of the iris

options.label: D
options.text: scotopsin

options.label: E
options.text: aqueous humour

questions.why: Vitamin A supplies retinal, historically called retinine-1. Its 11-cis form binds opsin in visual pigments. Light changes its configuration and triggers the phototransduction cascade.

notes.A: Somatostatin is a peptide hormone synthesised from amino acids, rather than from vitamin A.
notes.C: Iris colour is mainly determined by melanin and tissue optics. Retinal is a chromophore in photoreceptors.
notes.D: Scotopsin is the rod opsin protein, made from amino acids. Vitamin A supplies the retinal chromophore that binds it.
notes.E: Aqueous humour is produced by the ciliary processes through fluid and solute transport.

questions.stem: Intraocular fluid includes:

options.label: A
options.text: lens

options.label: B
options.text: aqueous humour

options.label: C
options.text: cornea

options.label: D
options.text: vitreous humour

options.label: E
options.text: ciliary body

questions.why: The aqueous humour is the fluid filling the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye.

notes.A: The lens is a solid structure.
notes.C: The cornea is solid tissue.
notes.D: Vitreous is a gel, not the circulating intraocular fluid.
notes.E: The ciliary body secretes aqueous.

questions.stem: The retina:

options.label: A
options.text: allows vision in light and dark, using cones and rods

options.label: B
options.text: gives depth perception using binocular vision

options.label: C
options.text: contains the ciliary muscles that control the shape of the lens

options.label: D
options.text: protects and supports the shape of the eye

options.label: E
options.text: controls colour vision

questions.why: The retina contains rods for sensitive vision in dim light and cones that support detail and colour in brighter conditions. Retinal circuits process the resulting signals before ganglion cells send information to the brain.

notes.B: The retina supplies signals from each eye. Binocular depth perception requires the brain to compare the two views.
notes.C: The ciliary muscles are in the ciliary body, anterior to the retina, and alter lens shape during accommodation.
notes.D: The sclera provides structural protection and helps maintain the shape of the globe. The retina is the sensory lining.
notes.E: Cones provide the initial wavelength signals used for colour, but colour perception also requires comparisons in retinal and central circuits. The retina also supports dim-light vision.

questions.stem: The portion of the fibrous layer of the eyeball that is white and opaque is the:

options.label: A
options.text: choroid

options.label: B
options.text: cornea

options.label: C
options.text: retina

options.label: D
options.text: sclera

options.label: E
options.text: iris

questions.why: The sclera is the tough, white, opaque portion of the outer fibrous coat of the eye. It is continuous anteriorly with the transparent cornea.

notes.A: The choroid is a vascular, pigmented layer between retina and sclera. It is not part of the white fibrous coat.
notes.B: The cornea forms the transparent anterior part of the fibrous coat and provides much of the eye's refraction.
notes.C: The retina is the inner neural and photoreceptive layer, rather than the fibrous outer wall.
notes.E: The iris is the pigmented structure that controls pupil size and is part of the vascular coat.

questions.stem: Nearsightedness is more properly called:

options.label: A
options.text: myopia

options.label: B
options.text: hyperopia

options.label: C
options.text: presbyopia

options.label: D
options.text: emmetropia

options.label: E
options.text: astigmatismus

questions.why: Myopia is short-sightedness. With accommodation relaxed, rays from a distant object are focused in front of the retina, often because the eye is too long or its refractive power is too strong.

notes.B: In hyperopia, distant rays tend to focus behind the retina when accommodation is relaxed. A converging lens can correct the error.
notes.C: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation that makes close focusing more difficult.
notes.D: Emmetropia is the state in which distant rays focus on the retina without accommodation.
notes.E: Astigmatism involves unequal refractive power in different meridians and can blur images at multiple distances.

questions.stem: Adaptation for vision in poor light is:

options.label: A
options.text: complete after 2-3 minutes

options.label: B
options.text: due mainly to dilatation of the pupil

options.label: C
options.text: due to regeneration of rod but not cone pigments

options.label: D
options.text: slower if red goggles are worn before entering the dark environment

options.label: E
options.text: more effective for peripheral than for central vision

questions.why: Rods dominate vision in very dim light and are abundant outside the rod-free central fovea. As rod sensitivity recovers in darkness, faint objects are easier to see slightly off-centre.

notes.A: Cone adaptation occurs early, but rod sensitivity continues to improve for much longer than two or three minutes.
notes.B: Pupil dilation increases retinal illumination, but it is too rapid and too limited to explain the full increase in retinal sensitivity.
notes.C: Both cone and rod photopigment systems adapt. Rods dominate the later phase and provide the greater sensitivity in low light.
notes.D: Red filters reduce stimulation of rods relative to many brighter broad-spectrum exposures, which can help preserve dark adaptation.

questions.stem: The cones in the retina differ from rods in that they are:

options.label: A
options.text: more numerous

options.label: B
options.text: more concerned with colour vision and high visual acuity

options.label: C
options.text: more sensitive to light

options.label: D
options.text: not concerned with high visual acuity

options.label: E
options.text: more affected by vitamin a deficiency

questions.why: Cones mediate colour vision and high acuity in good light. Central foveal cones are densely packed and have little convergence onto downstream cells, supporting fine spatial detail.

notes.A: The retina contains more rods than cones overall, although the central fovea contains cones and no rods.
notes.C: Rods are more sensitive to dim light. Cones generally need brighter illumination to mediate fine detail and colour.
notes.D: The cone-rich fovea provides the highest spatial acuity of the retina in good light.
notes.E: Both classes use retinal derived from vitamin A, but night blindness from impaired rod function is a characteristic early symptom of deficiency.

questions.stem: On entering a darkened room, the:

options.label: A
options.text: light intensity threshold of the eye starts to rise

options.label: B
options.text: final phase of retinal adaptation is mainly in the cones

options.label: C
options.text: final phase of retinal adaptation is mainly in the rods

options.label: D
options.text: adaptation is quicker if a long period was spent in bright light beforehand

options.label: E
options.text: time course for pupillary dilatation is similar to that for dark adaptation down to the adrenal medulla

questions.why: After a transition to darkness, cones adapt relatively quickly and then reach a plateau. Rod sensitivity recovers more slowly and is responsible for the late fall in the threshold for detecting light.

notes.A: The detection threshold falls as sensitivity increases. Progressively dimmer stimuli become visible.
notes.B: Cones contribute mainly to the early phase. Rods provide the greatest sensitivity in the late phase.
notes.D: Bright prior illumination can bleach more visual pigment. It generally delays recovery of full rod sensitivity.
notes.E: Pupil dilation is much faster than full dark adaptation. The slower increase in sensitivity depends on retinal changes.

questions.stem: Dilation of the pupil:

options.label: A
options.text: increases the amount of light entering the eye and the spherical aberration

options.label: B
options.text: increases the refractive power of the eye

options.label: C
options.text: decreases the spherical aberration

options.label: D
options.text: increases the depth of focus

options.label: E
options.text: increases the field of vision

questions.why: A wider pupil lets more light enter and admits more peripheral rays. Those rays are generally less well focused by the optical system, which increases the effect of spherical aberration.

notes.B: Changing aperture alters the bundle of rays entering the eye. It does not itself increase the optical power of the cornea or lens.
notes.C: A wider pupil admits more marginal rays, so spherical aberration generally has a greater rather than smaller effect.
notes.D: Depth of focus decreases when the pupil widens, so modest defocus is more noticeable.
notes.E: The main change is light entry and optical blur. The visual field is chiefly limited by retinal extent and ocular anatomy.

questions.stem: During accommodation for near vision:

options.label: A
options.text: more light enters the eye

options.label: B
options.text: the curvature of the cornea increases

options.label: C
options.text: chromatic and spherical aberration is decreased and the depth of focus increases

options.label: D
options.text: the depth of focus decreases

options.label: E
options.text: the visual axes of the two eyes diverge

questions.why: The near response increases lens curvature, converges the visual axes and constricts the pupils. A smaller pupil increases depth of focus and reduces image blur from spherical and chromatic aberrations, even though wavelength-dependent refraction still exists.

notes.A: Near fixation usually constricts the pupil, reducing the amount of incoming light at the same illumination.
notes.B: The lens becomes more convex as zonular tension falls. The cornea does not normally change curvature as the main accommodation mechanism.
notes.D: Pupil constriction increases depth of focus, allowing a slightly greater range of object distances to appear sharp.
notes.E: Convergence occurs when both eyes turn inward to fixate the same near target.

questions.stem: Visual acuity is:

options.label: A
options.text: a measure of the sensitivity of the retina to light

options.label: B
options.text: greater in a person with 0.5 vision than in one with 0.75

options.label: C
options.text: greater using central rather than peripheral vision

options.label: D
options.text: greater using one eye than both eyes

options.label: E
options.text: greater in normal than in colour-blind people

questions.why: Visual acuity measures the ability to resolve fine spatial detail. It is greatest with central foveal vision in adequate light because tightly packed cones and low neural convergence preserve spatial information.

notes.A: Sensitivity to very dim light is a detection threshold, which is different from resolving two nearby details.
notes.B: On a decimal acuity scale, 0.75 represents better resolution than 0.5.
notes.D: Binocular viewing usually provides comparable or somewhat better acuity than monocular viewing when both eyes function well.
notes.E: Common red–green colour vision deficiency can occur with otherwise normal spatial acuity.

questions.stem: In the refracting system of the eye:

options.label: A
options.text: the cornea causes less refraction than the lens

options.label: B
options.text: more refraction occurs at the inner surface of the cornea than at the outer surface

options.label: C
options.text: the lens, by becoming more convex, can more than double the total refractive power of the eye

options.label: D
options.text: the back surface of the lens contributes more to accommodation than the front

options.label: E
options.text: aging reduces the maximum refractive power of the eye

questions.why: Age-related stiffening of the lens reduces its ability to increase curvature during near accommodation. The maximum extra refractive power therefore falls, even when distance refraction has changed little.

notes.A: The cornea provides most of the eye's resting refractive power. The lens provides the major adjustable component.
notes.B: The largest refractive index change is at the outer air–cornea surface. The back surface contributes much less net refraction.
notes.C: Accommodation can add several dioptres in a young eye. It does not ordinarily double the total power of the cornea and lens.
notes.D: The anterior lens surface changes curvature more markedly during ordinary accommodation than the posterior surface.

questions.stem: When light is directed to one eye, the pupil:

options.label: A
options.text: constricts even though its optic nerve has been cut

options.label: B
options.text: responds due to sympathetic nerve activity

options.label: C
options.text: does not respond if autonomic cholinergic nerves are blocked by local application of atropine or if there is brainstem death

options.label: D
options.text: In that eye constricts and the opposite pupil dilates

options.label: E
options.text: respond if instead brainstem is death

questions.why: The pupillary light reflex depends on an intact retina and optic nerve, midbrain connections, and parasympathetic output to the iris sphincter. Local atropine blocks the muscarinic response in the treated eye. Brainstem death abolishes the reflex.

notes.A: Cutting the illuminated eye's optic nerve interrupts its afferent response. Its pupil can still constrict consensually if the intact opposite eye is illuminated.
notes.B: Sympathetic activity acts chiefly on the pupillary dilator. Constriction to light is mediated by parasympathetic nerves.
notes.D: In the normal light reflex, the illuminated pupil and the opposite pupil both constrict because the midbrain pathway projects bilaterally.
notes.E: Brainstem death abolishes this brainstem reflex. The pupils do not constrict in response to light.

questions.stem: Light from an object to the right of the visual axis:

options.label: A
options.text: impinges on the retina in the right eye to the right of the fovea

options.label: B
options.text: impinges on the retina in the left eye to the left of the fovea

options.label: C
options.text: generates impulses which produce conscious sensation in the frontal lobe eye fields

options.label: D
options.text: forms an inverted image on the retina

options.label: E
options.text: b, and d

questions.why: The cornea and lens produce a retinal image inverted vertically and reversed horizontally. An object in the right visual field is therefore projected to the left of each fovea, on nasal retina in the right eye and temporal retina in the left.

notes.A: In the right eye the image falls on the nasal side of the fovea, which is to its left in visual coordinates.
notes.B: In the left eye, a right-field image is formed on temporal hemiretina, physically to the left of that eye’s fovea.
notes.C: Conscious visual perception depends on occipital visual cortex and associated areas. Frontal eye fields chiefly help direct gaze.
notes.D: The optical system produces an inverted and horizontally reversed retinal image.

questions.stem: The rods in the retina:

options.label: A
options.text: contain visual pigment which is more sensitive to red than to blue light

options.label: B
options.text: are rendered sensitive by ordinary daylight

options.label: C
options.text: are more widely distributed over the retina than are cones

options.label: D
options.text: reflect blue light more than red light

options.label: E
options.text: comprise about 20 per cent of foveal receptor cells

questions.why: Rods are spread widely across the retina and are especially numerous outside the central fovea. The foveal centre contains densely packed cones and no rods, making rods particularly important for dim peripheral vision.

notes.A: Rhodopsin is most sensitive near the blue–green region and has relatively low sensitivity to long red wavelengths.
notes.B: Bright daylight can saturate rods and bleach their pigment. Rod sensitivity recovers during dark adaptation.
notes.D: Rod sensitivity reflects light absorption by rhodopsin. Preferential reflection is not the mechanism of phototransduction.
notes.E: The foveal centre contains cones and no rods. The proportion of rods increases away from the centre.

questions.stem: Cones:

options.label: A
options.text: are found in the most superficial layer of the retina

options.label: B
options.text: show a graded depolarization in response to light

options.label: C
options.text: contain pigments which are more light- sensitive than the rod pigment

options.label: D
options.text: contain pigments which are most affected by yellow-green light

options.label: E
options.text: are absent in an individual with colour blindness

questions.why: Cones are most sensitive to the yellow-green portion of the spectrum (around 555 nm).

notes.A: Photoreceptors are in the outermost (deepest) layer.
notes.B: Photoreceptors HYPERpolarise.
notes.C: Rod pigment is more sensitive.
notes.E: Usually one cone type is defective, not all absent.

questions.stem: Rhodopsin, the pigment of the rods is:

options.label: A
options.text: a yellow pigment

options.label: B
options.text: highly absorbent of red light

options.label: C
options.text: most sensitive to violet light

options.label: D
options.text: regenerated in the dark and least sensitive to red light

options.label: E
options.text: not regenerated in the dark and least sensitive to blue light

questions.why: Rhodopsin is the rod pigment formed by opsin and 11-cis retinal. After bleaching by light it regenerates during dark adaptation. It absorbs blue–green light most strongly and is relatively insensitive to long red wavelengths.

notes.A: Rhodopsin is traditionally called visual purple because of its appearance, not a yellow visual pigment.
notes.B: Long red wavelengths are relatively inefficient at activating rhodopsin compared with blue–green wavelengths.
notes.C: Rod pigment has its main sensitivity peak near 500 nm, in the blue–green region rather than violet.
notes.E: Darkness allows rhodopsin regeneration after bleaching, and blue–green light can be absorbed effectively.

questions.stem: In the visual field of the left eye, an object:

options.label: A
options.text: in the upper temporal quadrant is detected in the lower nasal quadrant of the retina

options.label: B
options.text: at the centre of the field of vision is detected in the optic disc

options.label: C
options.text: focused on the blind spot is in the nasal half of the visual field

options.label: D
options.text: in the temporal half generates impulses which travel the left optic tract

options.label: E
options.text: in the temporal half is more likely to be perceived in binocular vision than one in the nasal half

questions.why: The optics of the eye invert the image vertically and horizontally. A target in the upper temporal visual field of the left eye therefore projects to its lower nasal retina.

notes.B: The centre of the visual field is normally projected onto the fovea, where acuity is best. The optic disc has no photoreceptors.
notes.C: The optic disc lies nasal to the fovea and produces a blind spot in the temporal visual field.
notes.D: Fibres from left nasal retina cross at the chiasm. Left temporal-field information is therefore carried in the right optic tract.
notes.E: The far temporal crescent can be monocular because of the nose and orbital geometry. The nasal field usually overlaps with the other eye over a wide range.

questions.stem: In someone with short-sightedness (myopia):

options.label: A
options.text: the eye tends to be longer than average from lens to retina

options.label: B
options.text: a convex lens is required to correct the refractive error

options.label: C
options.text: close vision is affected more than distance vision

options.label: D
options.text: the near-point is farther than normal from the eye

options.label: E
options.text: a circular object tends to appear oval

questions.why: Axial myopia commonly results from an eye that is too long for its refractive power. Parallel rays from a distant object then come to a focus in front of the retina when accommodation is relaxed.

notes.B: A concave diverging lens shifts the focus of distant rays backward toward the retina.
notes.C: Distance vision is usually blurred more than near vision in uncorrected myopia.
notes.D: An uncorrected myopic eye commonly has a closer far point. The near point also depends on the available accommodative amplitude.
notes.E: An oval or directionally distorted image is more suggestive of unequal meridional focus, as in astigmatism, than simple myopia.

questions.stem: Colour blindness:

options.label: A
options.text: results from inability to detect one of three primary colours: red, yellow and blue

options.label: B
options.text: where red and green are indistinguishable is due to failure of red or green cone systems

options.label: C
options.text: in which no colours can be detected is the commonest form

options.label: D
options.text: is more common in women than men

options.label: E
options.text: is a disability linked to the Y-chromosome

questions.why: Common red–green colour vision deficiencies arise from absent or altered long- or medium-wavelength cone pigments. They reduce the ability to distinguish hues that normally produce different signals in the two cone classes.

notes.A: The three cone classes are most sensitive to long, medium or short wavelengths. There is no separate cone class with a specific yellow pigment.
notes.C: Complete absence of normal colour discrimination is uncommon. Red–green deficiencies are much more frequent.
notes.D: Common inherited red–green deficiencies are more frequent in males because the relevant opsin genes are X-linked.
notes.E: The principal long- and medium-wavelength opsin genes are on the X chromosome, rather than the Y chromosome.

questions.stem: Local application of atropine to the eye causes:

options.label: A
options.text: dilation of the pupil and reduced drainage of aqueous humour

options.label: B
options.text: the near-point for clear vision to move closer to the eye

options.label: C
options.text: inability to focus on objects at infinity

options.label: D
options.text: dilation of the pupil and increased drainage of aqueous humour

options.label: E
options.text: difficulty in looking upwards

questions.why: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist. It paralyzes the ciliary muscle (cycloplegia) and dilates the pupil (mydriasis). Pupil dilation can narrow the iridocorneal angle, reducing aqueous drainage and potentially triggering glaucoma.

notes.B: The near point moves FARTHER (cycloplegia).
notes.C: Distance vision is kept; near vision is lost.
notes.D: Drainage is REDUCED.
notes.E: Atropine does not affect the extraocular muscles.

questions.stem: Interruption of the visual pathway in the:

options.label: A
options.text: left optic tract causes blindness in the right visual field (right homonymous hemianopia)

options.label: B
options.text: optic chiasma causes blindness in the nasal half of each visual field (binasal hemianopia)

options.label: C
options.text: left optic radiation causes loss of vision to the left

options.label: D
options.text: occipital cortex causes loss of the light reflex

options.label: E
options.text: occipital cortex causes loss of central vision with preservation of peripheral vision

questions.why: The left optic tract carries signals from the right visual field of both eyes. It contains crossed right nasal retinal fibres and uncrossed left temporal retinal fibres. A complete left tract lesion therefore causes right homonymous hemianopia.

notes.B: A central chiasmal lesion damages crossing nasal retinal fibres and usually causes bitemporal, rather than binasal, field loss.
notes.C: Left optic radiations carry right visual-field information. The pattern depends on whether the lesion affects the full tract or only part of it.
notes.D: Pupillary light reflex fibres branch to the pretectal region before the visual cortex, so an isolated occipital lesion can spare the light reflex.
notes.E: An occipital lesion often causes a contralateral field defect. Some lesions preserve central vision instead of selectively removing it.

questions.stem: Squinting (strabismus) may result from:

options.label: A
options.text: poor vision in one eye in childhood or a refractive error in childhood

options.label: B
options.text: damage to the posterior pituitary

options.label: C
options.text: central suppression of vision in one eye in childhood

options.label: D
options.text: damage to the cerebellum

options.label: E
options.text: damage to the external capsule

questions.why: Strabismus often results from uncorrected refractive errors or poor vision in one eye during childhood, disrupting binocular alignment.

notes.B: The pituitary does not move the eyes.
notes.C: This is a result of squint (amblyopia), not a cause.
notes.D: Cerebellar damage causes nystagmus, not squint.
notes.E: The external capsule is not involved.

questions.stem: Impairment of visual acuity in bright light can be explained by:

options.label: A
options.text: random light scattering when there is dense pigmentation of the eye

options.label: B
options.text: random light scattering when there is asymmetrical corneal curvature due to astigmatism

options.label: C
options.text: random light scattering in the cornea when there is vitamin A deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: impairment of rod function when there is vitamin A deficiency

options.label: E
options.text: inability to alter the focal length of the lens when a cataract is present

questions.why: Severe vitamin A deficiency can cause xerophthalmia and corneal surface damage. A rough or opaque cornea scatters light and reduces acuity even in bright illumination, when vision normally depends largely on cones.

notes.A: Iris and choroidal pigment generally reduce stray light. Dense pigmentation does not normally generate the corneal scatter described.
notes.B: Astigmatism causes unequal focusing in different meridians. The blur does not chiefly arise from randomly scattered light.
notes.D: Rod dysfunction in vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness. It does not explain the bright-light acuity loss as well as corneal damage.
notes.E: Cataract decreases acuity mainly through lens opacity and light scatter. Loss of accommodation primarily affects near focusing.

questions.stem: In long-sightedness (hypermetropia):

options.label: A
options.text: objects at infinity cannot be focused sharply on the retina

options.label: B
options.text: objects at the usual near-point are focused in front of the retina

options.label: C
options.text: ciliary muscle contracts more strongly to bring objects in mid- visual range into clear focus

options.label: D
options.text: the range of unblurred vision (near-point to far-point) is greater than normal

options.label: E
options.text: the near-point can be brought closer to the eye by the use of a biconcave lens

questions.why: In hypermetropia, the eye's refractive power is insufficient relative to its length when accommodation is relaxed. An eye with enough ciliary reserve can increase lens curvature to bring targets into focus, so it may accommodate even for intermediate or distant vision.

notes.A: A hypermetropic eye with relaxed accommodation focuses parallel rays behind the retina, but a young person may compensate by accommodating.
notes.B: With inadequate accommodation, rays from a near object are focused behind the retina rather than in front of it.
notes.D: Hypermetropia can use up part of the accommodative reserve even for distance and may move the near point farther away.
notes.E: A convex converging lens supplies extra positive power. A concave lens would increase the focusing problem.

questions.stem: What controls not only hearing but also a sense of gravity and motion:

options.label: A
options.text: the incus and the stapes

options.label: B
options.text: the pinna and the ear drum

options.label: C
options.text: the vestibular nerve and the semi circular canals

options.label: D
options.text: the eustachian tube and the stapes

options.label: E
options.text: the mesencephalon

questions.why: The vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals, utricle, saccule) and the vestibular nerve mediate balance and spatial orientation.

notes.A: The ossicles serve hearing only.
notes.B: These serve hearing only.
notes.D: The tube equalises pressure.
notes.E: The midbrain is not a sense organ.

questions.stem: Hair cells in the ear:

options.label: A
options.text: are sensory receptors that fire action potentials when they are disturbed

options.label: B
options.text: show a graded response, instead of the spikes typical of other neurons

options.label: C
options.text: are bent against the overhanging tectorial membrane

options.label: D
options.text: b, and c

options.label: E
options.text: a, b, and c

questions.why: Hair cells give graded receptor potentials, not action potentials. Bending of their stereocilia against the tectorial membrane opens mechanically gated channels, and they release glutamate onto the cochlear nerve fibres, which then fire.

notes.A: Hair cells give graded potentials; the nerve fibres fire.
notes.B: True, but so is C.
notes.C: True, but so is B.
notes.E: A is false.

questions.stem: The transmission of sound vibrations through the internal ear occurs mainly through the:

options.label: A
options.text: nerve fibers

options.label: B
options.text: air

options.label: C
options.text: fluid

options.label: D
options.text: bone

options.label: E
options.text: cartilage

questions.why: Movement of the stapes at the oval window creates pressure waves in cochlear fluid. Differences in fluid pressure move the cochlear partition, and hair cells later convert this mechanical input to electrical signalling.

notes.A: Auditory fibres carry neural signals after transduction. Mechanical vibration travels through cochlear fluid before that step.
notes.B: Sound reaches the outer and middle ear through air, but the cochlear spaces are filled with liquid.
notes.D: Bone can conduct sound to the cochlea by an alternative route. The main movement inside the cochlea is transmitted through fluid.
notes.E: Cartilage contributes to structures of the external ear. It is not the principal medium inside the cochlea.

questions.stem: Which of the following is important in maintaining the balance of the body?

options.label: A
options.text: visual cues

options.label: B
options.text: semicircular canals

options.label: C
options.text: the saccule

options.label: D
options.text: proprioceptors

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Balance depends on integrated visual, vestibular and proprioceptive input. The semicircular canals detect angular acceleration, the saccule senses linear acceleration and position relative to gravity, and proprioceptors indicate body and limb position.

notes.A: Visual information helps determine body motion and orientation relative to the surroundings.
notes.B: Rotations are detected by the semicircular canals through movement of endolymph and displacement of the cupula.
notes.C: The saccule is an otolith organ that responds to linear acceleration and gravitational forces, particularly in a roughly vertical plane.
notes.D: Muscle and joint proprioceptors provide information about limb position, movement and contact with the support surface.

questions.stem: The basilar membrane of the cochlea vibrates:

options.label: A
options.text: at the same frequency as the applied sound

options.label: B
options.text: with an amplitude which is proportional to the frequency of the applied sound

options.label: C
options.text: with an amplitude which is counter proportional to the loudness of the applied sound

options.label: D
options.text: more along of its length when the applied sound has a high rather than low frequency

options.label: E
options.text: mainly at the base of the cochlea for the sound frequencies commonly used in speech

questions.why: A pure tone drives basilar membrane motion at the frequency of that tone. The point of greatest displacement varies with frequency, with higher frequencies peaking near the base and lower frequencies closer to the apex.

notes.B: A higher frequency moves the peak toward the base. The size of the displacement is also influenced by sound level and cochlear mechanics.
notes.C: Increasing sound level generally increases displacement, with nonlinear compression over parts of the range. The relationship is not inverse.
notes.D: High-frequency waves peak nearer the base and decay before reaching much of the apical cochlea. Low-frequency waves travel farther apically.
notes.E: Speech contains a wide range of frequencies, which excite different regions of the cochlea rather than mainly the extreme base.

questions.stem: The tympanic membrane:

options.label: A
options.text: modifies the frequencies of sound waves impinging on the ear

options.label: B
options.text: stops vibrating almost immediately after the sound stops

options.label: C
options.text: bulges outwards when the pharyngotympanic tube is blocked

options.label: D
options.text: transmits sound more effectively when the small muscles of the middle ear are contracted

options.label: E
options.text: continues to vibtate after the sound stops

questions.why: The tympanic membrane follows the pattern of pressure changes in incoming sound. Damping in the membrane and middle-ear system causes the resulting vibration to decay rapidly when the stimulus stops.

notes.A: The membrane and ossicles transmit the frequency components of sound. Their efficiency varies with frequency, but they do not normally change those frequencies.
notes.C: Eustachian tube obstruction commonly lowers middle-ear pressure as gas is absorbed. Higher external pressure then tends to retract the membrane inward.
notes.D: Contraction of middle-ear muscles generally stiffens the transmission system and attenuates some sound, especially at lower frequencies.
notes.E: Any residual ringing is brief because the system is damped. A sustained vibration after sound stops is not expected.

questions.stem: The hair cells in the semicircular canals are stimulated by:

options.label: A
options.text: movement of perilymph

options.label: B
options.text: linear acceleration

options.label: C
options.text: rotation at constant velocity

options.label: D
options.text: gravity

options.label: E
options.text: movement of endolymph relative to hair cells

questions.why: When the head starts rotating, inertia causes endolymph to move relative to the canal wall. The resulting cupula displacement bends hair-cell stereocilia and changes vestibular nerve activity.

notes.A: The fluid inside the membranous semicircular ducts is endolymph, which acts on the cupula.
notes.B: Linear acceleration is detected principally by the utricle and saccule, rather than by the semicircular canals.
notes.C: At constant rotational velocity, endolymph eventually moves with the canal and cupula deflection subsides. The initial change in rotation is the effective stimulus.
notes.D: Gravity acts on the otolith membranes of the utricle and saccule. Semicircular canals normally detect angular acceleration.

questions.stem: The tympanic membranes:

options.label: A
options.text: bulge outwards during descent in an unpressurized airplane

options.label: B
options.text: have an area about twice that of the oval window

options.label: C
options.text: prevent sound waves from reaching the oval and round windows at the same time

options.label: D
options.text: transmit only 10 per cent of applied sound energy to the cochlea for sound waves of 1000 Hz

options.label: E
options.text: transmit sounds in the 500-5000 Hz frequency range with the least loss of energy

questions.why: The middle ear system ensures that sound waves reach the oval window slightly before the round window, allowing the fluid to move.

notes.A: During descent it bulges INWARD.
notes.B: It is about 17 times larger.
notes.D: Transmission is about 60%.
notes.E: Not its defining role.

questions.stem: Sound waves:

options.label: A
options.text: are quantified on the decibel scale, which is logarithmic

options.label: B
options.text: with an intensity of 60 decibels are inaudible

options.label: C
options.text: with an intensity of 140 decibels are harmless

options.label: D
options.text: with an intensity of 90 decibels are usually painful

options.label: E
options.text: are heard as a note one octave higher when their frequency increases eight-fold

questions.why: Sound pressure level is usually expressed in decibels on a logarithmic scale. An increase in decibels corresponds to a multiplicative change in sound pressure or intensity rather than a linear one.

notes.B: A level of 60 decibels is commonly comparable to ordinary conversation and is clearly audible to most people with normal hearing.
notes.C: Sound near 140 decibels can cause severe hearing injury and may reach or exceed the pain threshold.
notes.D: A 90-decibel sound can be hazardous with prolonged exposure, but it is usually below the threshold of pain.
notes.E: An octave is a twofold increase in frequency. An eightfold increase corresponds to three octaves.

questions.stem: The frequency of impulses generated by receptors in an utricle is:

options.label: A
options.text: related to the orientation of the head and reduced in the weightless conditions in outer space

options.label: B
options.text: higher during travel at 100 than at 20 miles per hour

options.label: C
options.text: not related to the orientation of the head and increased in the weightless conditions in outer space

options.label: D
options.text: inversely related to the frequency being generated by the opposite utricle

options.label: E
options.text: related to the impulse frequency being generated by semicircular canal receptors

questions.why: The utricle detects linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity. In weightlessness (microgravity), the otoliths don't press on the hair cells, reducing the impulse frequency.

notes.B: Constant velocity gives no signal.
notes.C: Firing IS related to head orientation.
notes.D: The two utricles are not simply reciprocal.
notes.E: They are independent sensors.

questions.stem: An audiogram:

options.label: A
options.text: is a plot of hearing ability (or hearing loss) against sound frequency

options.label: B
options.text: showing equal impairment of air and bone conduction suggests conductive deafness

options.label: C
options.text: showing hearing loss at high frequencies for air conduction suggests ear drum damage

options.label: D
options.text: showing loss at 8000 Hz for air and bone conduction suggests conductive deafness

options.label: E
options.text: showing hearing loss at the lower frequencies is common in elderly people

questions.why: An audiogram plots hearing thresholds in decibels against sound frequency. Comparing air and bone conduction helps distinguish impaired transmission through the outer or middle ear from cochlear or neural hearing loss.

notes.B: In sensorineural loss, both air and bone thresholds are elevated without a significant air–bone gap.
notes.C: An air-conduction loss alone does not localise the lesion to the tympanic membrane. Bone thresholds and middle-ear findings are also needed.
notes.D: When both air and bone thresholds are elevated at a high frequency, a sensorineural component is likely.
notes.E: Typical age-related hearing loss affects high frequencies first, although hearing patterns vary.

questions.stem: In the middle ear:

options.label: A
options.text: destruction of the auditory ossicles abolishes hearing

options.label: B
options.text: paralysis of the auditory muscles makes sounds more faint

options.label: C
options.text: immobilization of the stapes causes smaller deafness than removal of the ossicles

options.label: D
options.text: air pressure is normally atmospheric pressure

options.label: E
options.text: the round window doesn’t move reciprocally with the oval window

questions.why: The Eustachian tube intermittently opens to equalise pressure between the middle ear and the nasopharynx. At normal equilibrium, middle-ear air pressure is therefore close to atmospheric pressure.

notes.A: Ossicular disruption causes conductive hearing loss. Bone conduction can still stimulate the cochlea, so hearing is not necessarily abolished.
notes.B: The middle-ear muscles can attenuate transmission of intense sound. Losing this action does not generally make sound fainter.
notes.C: Stapes fixation and ossicular loss both cause conductive impairment. The degree depends on the exact mechanical defect.
notes.E: Movement of the oval window displaces cochlear fluid, and the round window usually moves reciprocally to accommodate that displacement.

questions.stem: Involuntary oscillatory eye movements (nystagmus):

options.label: A
options.text: do not occur in healthy people

options.label: B
options.text: may result from cochlear disease

options.label: C
options.text: occur in cerebellar disease and when hot fluid is run into one external ear canal

options.label: D
options.text: occur when fluid at body temperature is run into one external ear canal

options.label: E
options.text: do not affect acuity of vision

questions.why: Cerebellar disorders can disrupt gaze stability and produce nystagmus. Warming one external ear canal can also produce caloric nystagmus by stimulating the vestibular apparatus. These mechanisms are distinct but both affect eye movements.

notes.A: Physiological nystagmus can occur in healthy people during rotation, caloric stimulation or optokinetic testing.
notes.B: The cochlea serves hearing, whereas vestibular dysfunction drives vestibular nystagmus. Disorders can affect both structures, but isolated cochlear disease is not the typical mechanism.
notes.D: Fluid at body temperature produces little thermal gradient and does not normally elicit a substantial caloric response.
notes.E: Persistent nystagmus can blur vision or decrease acuity by making it difficult to hold an image on the fovea.

questions.stem: Taste receptors:

options.label: A
options.text: for sweet, sour, salt and bitter are spatially separated on the surface of the tongue

options.label: B
options.text: are synonymous with taste buds

options.label: C
options.text: are a type of chemoreceptors

options.label: D
options.text: are innervated by afferents in the facial, trigeminal and glossopharyngeal nerves

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Taste receptor cells are chemoreceptors that respond to dissolved substances reaching the taste pore. Their activity stimulates afferent fibres in cranial nerves VII, IX and X.

notes.A: Multiple taste qualities can be detected in different parts of the tongue. There is no strict spatial map assigning each taste to one region.
notes.B: A taste bud is a group of specialised cells, including several receptor and support cell types. A receptor cell is one part of the bud.
notes.D: The trigeminal nerve carries touch, temperature and irritation from much of the mouth. Standard taste afferents travel mainly in VII, IX and X.
notes.E: The strict tongue map is inaccurate, and trigeminal fibres are not standard primary taste afferents.

questions.stem: The sense that certain foods are sweet is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: fungiform papillae

options.label: B
options.text: taste buds of the soft palate

options.label: C
options.text: foliate papillae

options.label: D
options.text: circumvallate papillae

options.label: E
options.text: all of the above

questions.why: Sweet-sensitive receptor cells are present in taste buds across multiple oral regions. Fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae can all contribute, and taste buds on the soft palate can also signal sweetness.

notes.A: Fungiform papillae on the anterior tongue contain taste buds that can detect sweet substances.
notes.B: Soft-palate taste buds can respond to sweet stimuli, contributing to taste outside the tongue.
notes.C: Foliate folds at the posterolateral tongue contain taste buds that can respond to several qualities, including sweetness.
notes.D: Circumvallate papillae at the back of the tongue contain taste buds. They are not restricted to bitter stimuli.

questions.stem: These receptors react to foods treated with monosodium glutamate:

options.label: A
options.text: salt

options.label: B
options.text: sour

options.label: C
options.text: bitter

options.label: D
options.text: sweet

options.label: E
options.text: umami

questions.why: The savoury taste elicited by glutamate in monosodium glutamate is umami. Glutamate can activate the T1R1–T1R3 taste receptor complex, and certain nucleotides enhance the response.

notes.A: MSG contains sodium, but glutamate gives it the characteristic savoury taste rather than a purely salty one.
notes.B: Sour taste is principally a response to acids and hydrogen ions. Glutamate is the defining stimulus in this comparison.
notes.C: Bitter compounds are detected through a separate family of receptors, rather than the main glutamate-sensitive receptor complex.
notes.D: The sweet receptor uses T1R2 with T1R3. The main umami receptor pairs T1R1 with T1R3.

questions.stem: Olfactory tract damage would probably affect the ability to?

options.label: A
options.text: see

options.label: B
options.text: hear

options.label: C
options.text: feel pain

options.label: D
options.text: smell

options.label: E
options.text: speak

questions.why: The olfactory tract carries output from the olfactory bulb toward primary olfactory regions. Damage can reduce or abolish the sense of smell on the affected side.

notes.A: Vision depends on the retina and optic pathways. It is not the primary sensory function of the olfactory tract.
notes.B: Hearing uses cochlear and central auditory pathways rather than the axons of the olfactory tract.
notes.C: Pain sensation is conveyed through nociceptive pathways. Nasal irritation can be detected separately by trigeminal fibres even when smell is impaired.
notes.E: Speech is supported by language and motor networks. The olfactory tract carries signals about odours.

questions.stem: Where are taste buds found?

options.label: A
options.text: anterior part of the tongue

options.label: B
options.text: posterior part of the tongue

options.label: C
options.text: palate

options.label: D
options.text: lips

options.label: E
options.text: a, b, and c

questions.why: Taste buds lie in several lingual papillae and in some sites outside the tongue, including the soft palate. The anterior and posterior tongue can both detect more than one taste quality.

notes.A: The anterior tongue contains taste buds mainly within fungiform papillae.
notes.B: Posterior taste buds are present in circumvallate and foliate papillae and contribute to several taste qualities.
notes.C: The soft palate has a smaller but recognised population of taste buds.
notes.D: The lips provide tactile and other somatic sensation. They are not a standard normal site of taste buds.

questions.stem: Cells in the olfactory bulb that act as local 'integrators' of olfactory inputs are the:

options.label: A
options.text: hair cells

options.label: B
options.text: granule cells

options.label: C
options.text: basal cells

options.label: D
options.text: mitral cells

options.label: E
options.text: supporting cells

questions.why: Mitral cells are the principal projection neurons of the olfactory bulb that integrate signals from olfactory receptor neurons.

notes.A: Hair cells are in the ear.
notes.B: Granule cells are inhibitory interneurons.
notes.C: Basal cells are stem cells in the epithelium.
notes.E: Supporting cells are in the epithelium.

questions.stem: Olfactory cells:

options.label: A
options.text: are epithelial cells which synapse with olfactory nerves

options.label: B
options.text: generate impulses when stimulated which are relayed in the thalamus

options.label: C
options.text: are chemoreceptors

options.label: D
options.text: show little adaptation

options.label: E
options.text: are less important than taste in appreciating the flavour of food

questions.why: Olfactory receptor cells are sensory neurons that respond chemically to airborne molecules dissolved in nasal mucus. Odorant binding at their cilia changes membrane activity and can generate action potentials that travel to the olfactory bulb.

notes.A: Olfactory receptor cells are neurons within the epithelium. Their own axons form olfactory nerve fibres and synapse within the bulb.
notes.B: The first synapse is in the olfactory bulb. Primary olfactory cortex can receive bulb output without an initial obligatory thalamic relay.
notes.D: Olfactory intensity can fade with sustained exposure through adaptation of peripheral and central responses.
notes.E: Retronasal smell is a major contributor to food flavour, interacting with taste and oral sensations.

questions.stem: Increasing the salt concentration applied to a 'salt' taste bud increases:

options.label: A
options.text: its sensitivity to salt

options.label: B
options.text: the amplitude of its generator potentials and impulse traffic to the thalamus

options.label: C
options.text: the amplitude of the action potentials generated

options.label: D
options.text: impulse traffic to the anterior pituitary

options.label: E
options.text: impulse traffic to the adrenal medulla

questions.why: Increasing salt concentration within a responsive range can produce a larger taste-cell receptor potential. This can increase transmitter release and the frequency of spikes in taste afferents, whose signals eventually reach the thalamus.

notes.A: A stronger response to a stronger stimulus does not necessarily mean the receptor has become more sensitive.
notes.C: Action potentials are all-or-none. Stimulus intensity is represented mainly by spike frequency and recruitment rather than spike size.
notes.D: Gustatory pathways relay through the brainstem to the thalamus and cortex. The anterior pituitary is not the primary relay.
notes.E: The adrenal medulla is a sympathetic effector. Taste information reaches central gustatory pathways rather than being conveyed to it as the main relay.

questions.stem: The olfactory system can detect:

options.label: A
options.text: only 20-40 distinct odours

options.label: B
options.text: the direction from which an odour comes and differences in odour between isomers of the same substance

options.label: C
options.text: odours equally well at all ages

options.label: D
options.text: small differences in the concentration of an odorant

options.label: E
options.text: odours better in old than in young people

questions.why: The olfactory system is highly sensitive and can distinguish between subtle differences in chemical structures (isomers).

notes.A: Thousands of odours can be detected.
notes.C: Smell declines with age.
notes.D: Concentration discrimination is poor (about 30%).
notes.E: Young people smell better.

questions.stem: The receptor cells serving taste:

options.label: A
options.text: are confined to the tongue

options.label: B
options.text: are stimulated when chemicals diffuse through the overlying epithelium to reach them

options.label: C
options.text: are primary sensory neurones

options.label: D
options.text: are histologically different for the four primary taste modalities

options.label: E
options.text: for sweetness are more common at the tip than at the back of the tongue

questions.why: Taste buds for sweetness are concentrated at the tip of the tongue (though modern science shows they are not exclusively there).

notes.A: They are also on the palate, pharynx and epiglottis.
notes.B: Chemicals reach them through the taste pore.
notes.C: They are modified epithelial cells.
notes.D: They look alike.
